title: The Yowie: Australia's Hairy Giant
description:
Deep in the ancient forests of eastern Australia — the Blue Mountains, the Queensland rainforest, the Gold Coast hinterland — people keep coming back with the same impossible story: a hairy man-beast, up to ten feet tall, covered in dark shaggy hair, with a terrible smell and enormous strength. Even today, the landscape is still changing.

title: The 1969 Apollo 11 Space Suit Was Made By Playtex
description:
Seriously someone needs to turn this into a movie!

The first men to walk on the moon were basically wearing a high-tech brassiere. Not even a little joking.

When NASA put out a bid in 1962 for the Apollo spacesuit, the expected winners were major defense contractors like your Hamilton Standard, Goodrich, Litton Industries. Then out of nowhere Playtex submitted a bid. A “bra” company.

Despite not having any aerospace experience, Playtex’s 21 layer hand stitched space suit blew all its competitors out of the water. 

The suit was built almost entirely by female seamstresses. Every stitch was done by hand because if even one stitch more than 1/64 of an inch off, then the suit failed inspection because a failed suit could mean an astronaut’s death.

Eleanor “Ellie” Foraker was in charge of this army of seamstresses. She went from the diaper-cover assembly line to NASA’s spacesuit assembly supervisor. She practically didn’t leave the plant for three years to ensure the safety of these space suits.

One small stitch for a man. One giant leap for mankind

Did you know about this story?

description:
GIANTS OF PREHISTORIC FRANCE? | 1894 Newspaper Report Claims 10–15 Foot Humans Near Montpellier

DESCRIPTION

An extraordinary newspaper report published in the Davenport Daily Leader on November 25, 1894 described a prehistoric cemetery reportedly uncovered near Montpellier, France, while workers were excavating for a waterworks reservoir.

According to the report, unusually large human skulls and bones were discovered, and the story claimed the remains belonged to a race of people estimated to have stood between 10 and 15 feet tall.

The article was part of a wave of late-19th-century newspaper stories describing alleged discoveries of giant human remains.

But there is an important distinction:

The newspaper reported the claim — that does not by itself prove that 10–15-foot humans were scientifically verified.

Stories like this are still fascinating because they preserve what newspapers, local observers, and early antiquarians were reporting at the time.

Questions worth investigating include:

Were the bones preserved?
Who measured them?
Was a French scientific report ever published?
Were the skull measurements accurately reported?
Did other newspapers copy the same original source?
